title: Getting Young Children to Stay in Bed and Sleep

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Research shows that about 30% of toddlers and pre-school children have trouble getting to sleep and staying asleep. Some of these problems can be considered normal, but when sleep disruption persists beyond a parent's ability to cope, the end result can be depressed parents and strained family relationships. Sleep problems can also affect children's later health and behaviour.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For this reason, it is essential that parents have workable sleep solutions that do no harm. 'Many exhausted parents need help, but don't want to use the commonly promoted methods based on controlled crying, because it's simply too distressing,' says paediatric sleep specialist Associate Professor Sarah Blunden, a view endorsed by her colleague Dr. Kirlithy Thompson, also of the Appleton Institute, Central Queensland University, Australia. 'Ignoring a young one's cry, even if only for two minutes, is like two hours for a mother. But parents who choose not to use these methods aren't being offered anything else.' Blunden and Thompson's new book, Boss of My Sleep, offers parents a way to teach their children to become independent sleepers without having to ignore their cries. It advocates putting the children themselves in charge of their bedtime.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Controlled crying, sometimes referred to as 'controlled comforting', is where parents attend to their young child at defined, increasing intervals, such as at two, five then ten minutes, until the child settles. 'Camping out' is when the parent sits close to a child as he or she falls asleep. Parents then move their seating position progressively nearer to the door while the child falls asleep. These methods are not recommended for infants less than six months old. 'There's no doubt that controlled comforting and camping out work-in that the baby or child will stop crying or calling out, usually within a few nights,' Blunden says. 'That might be fine for 50 to 60 percent of children but I'm concerned about the 35 to 40 percent of children who are stressed or anxious.'

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Dr. Anna Price from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute in Melbourne, Australia, was also aware of parents' concerns about controlled comforting approaches. She carried out a six-year randomised controlled study involving 225 children from seven months of age. The study showed that, compared with the control group, children who experienced controlled comforting or camping out were no more likely to have significantly poorer emotional health, sleep or behaviour problems, chronic stress, poor attachment with parents, depression or anxiety. These findings may succeed in allaying the concerns of parents, but do not make it any easier for them to use these approaches.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Changes in parenting styles could be disrupting children's sleep patterns, says Marie Clifford, manager at the Tresillian Family Care Centre in Wollstonecraft, North Sydney, Australia. 'Parents are much more flexible than they used to be, so consistent bedtime routines are often missing,' Clifford says. 'We have some parents saying they can't get their toddler to bed until midnight, and with more parents in paid work, there's greater pressure to get the child to sleep through the night at six weeks. Some parents keep the infant or child up until 9:00 pm to see dad when he gets home from work. By then the child is exhausted, but the parents may also need the child to be up again at the crack of dawn to get to daycare. A normal sleep pattern for a toddler should be 12-15 hours a day, including their daytime naps, but parents may try to fit too much into the child's waking hours, extending them far past the norm.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Daniel and Kim Maung of Fullarton, Adelaide, experienced the exhaustion that one toddler with sleep problems can cause, and decided to try the concepts introduced in Boss of My Sleep. 'When Brett was three it'd take us about an hour to get him to sleep,' says Mr Maung. 'Then he might wake up once or twice during the night and come into our room. When you have two working parents, you give in because you are so tired.' As a result, the Maungs were open to Blunden and Thompson's rewards-based approach, which harnesses toddlers' desire for independence.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The concept, explained in detail in Boss of My Sleep, involves rewarding the child with one sticker for completing his or her bedtime routine, then another sticker for waiting in bed all night. If the child earns two stickers by morning, then there's a simple prize or lots of praise and cuddles. Parents don't need to ignore a child's call-they can respond by calling back, reminding the child they are coming back at an agreed interval, but they need to wait in bed for them. 'If you ignore them, they will come out, so ignoring is pointless,' Blunden says. Toddlers can vote with their feet if they don't want to go to bed, but Brett was sold on his stickers and sleep book, thinking it was a fun game where he could win a prize. 'He didn't understand the end game was staying in bed,' Maung says. Within a few weeks Brett was going to bed and staying there all night without complaint. 'We were a bit worried about what would happen when we stopped the prizes,' Maung says, 'but that wasn't much of an issue as he had the confidence to be able to put himself to sleep. We told him how great it was that he was now the boss of his sleep, and he was happy with that.' He remains a good sleeper.

groups.title: The Boss of My Sleep concept
content: Under this scheme the child receives rewards in the form of stickers, leading to a prize. One of these is given when the child finishes his nightly {{24}} by getting into bed. The other is awarded if he remains in bed until the morning. Getting both is necessary for the prize. The parents check the child at fixed times and if he cries, they reassure him by calling out and telling him they will come after the arranged {{25}} . The approach is successful with young children because they see it as a {{26}} .
